newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS - Malaysia commodities seen hit by ringgit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Malaysia commodities seen hit by ringgit.

text.p: Malaysia's strong ringgit has hurt its rubber market, and the currency's rally could dent the nation's export competitiveness in commodities, traders and analysts said on Monday.
"Commodity producers will definitely be hit in terms of export competitiveness," said Vincent Low, an economist with Singapore-based J.P. Morgan.
"Export competitiveness in commodities will deteriorate faster," he warned.
Traders said the strong Malaysian currency has made local rubber too expensive to be competitive against Thai and Indonesian material.
"The prices must go down further, otherwise we'll be too much at a premium with Thailand and Indonesia," said a dealer with a foreign-owned rubber brokerage in Kuala Lumpur.
The rubber market, already in the doldrums since October due to weak consumer demand, has suffered falling prices since last week's ringgit surge against the U.S. dollar.

At Monday's midday market, the Malaysian Rubber Exchange and Licensing Board quoted February buyers of the benchmark Ribbed Smoke Sheet One at 305 cents ($1.23) a kilogram, down 10 cents from a week ago.
Buyers of February SMR20 were quoted at 303.50 cents a kg, down 6.50 cents in the same period.

The Malaysian ringgit has gained 500 points against the dollar in a week on strong speculative buying, spurred by the country's fundamentals and relatively high interest rates. The currency hit a 17-month high of 2.4690 to the dollar early on Monday, before slipping slightly later in the session.

A lot of rubber was sold in U.S. dollars and previous transactions showed many buyers did not hedge against the ringgit to prevent losses in the event of a jump in its value, the Kuala Lumper rubber dealer said.
The ringgit's five cent increase in recent days meant buyers who had purchased Malaysian rubber last week now stood to lose 50 ringgit for every tonne purchased, traders said.
"A buy-order could be anything from 20 tonnes to 200 tonnes. This means a loss of 1,000 ringgit to 10,000 ringgit in a week," said the rubber dealer.
Traders noted good weather since the start of January has created an ample supply of latex, which was adding to downward pressure on prices.

"Some buying and short-covering is still going on in Indonesia and Thailand," said another trader with a regional rubber broking house in Kuala Lumpur. "That's because their prices are around 10 (Malaysian) cents below any of ours."
But other agricultural commodities such as palm oil and cocoa were more likely to weather the currency rally, traders said.
Palm oil traders said they did not expect any major impact from the currency surge as the crop itself was traded in ringgit and in forward contracts.

"The forward (contract) months from March onwards may see a slight impact," said a palm oil trader. "If the ringgit is surging, this means that it will be too expensive for the buyers and bad for the exporters."
Cocoa was insulated from the ringgit's fluctuations as it was traded in futures and in British pounds, said officials for the crop.
"I don't really see an immediate impact but there could be some precaution if the trend continues," Malaysian Cocoa Board director-general Mohamed Musa Jamil told Reuters.
-- K. Baranee Krishnaan (603-230-7509) ($1=2.4810 ringgit)
